questions.prompt: Without an index on email, how does the database find the row WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'?

options.text: It reads every row in the table (a full table scan)
It jumps straight to the row using the primary key

questions.explanation: Without an index on the column, the only way to find matches is to read every row and check it.

questions.prompt: Why does a B-tree lookup among 100 million keys take only a few disk reads?

options.text: Each node holds hundreds of keys, so the tree is only three or four levels deep
B-trees hash the key directly to its location

questions.explanation: With a fan-out of hundreds, each level divides the search space by hundreds. Three levels of 500 cover 125 million keys.

questions.prompt: There's an index on (user_id, created_at). Which queries can use it efficiently? Select all that apply.

options.text: WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20

questions.explanation: The index is sorted by user_id first, then created_at. Queries that fix user_id can use it, including sorting by created_at within that user. Filtering on created_at alone can't, because those values are spread across every user.

questions.prompt: A table receives 20,000 inserts per second and has nine indexes. Inserts are slow. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: Each insert must also update nine index structures
Indexes make inserts skip the log

questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but every write must update each one. Remove indexes that no query uses.

questions.prompt: What does an LSM tree trade to get very fast writes?

options.text: Durability: recent writes can be lost
Reads may check several files, and background compaction rewrites data (write amplification)
It can't support range queries at all

questions.explanation: LSM trees append writes to a log and an in-memory buffer, then merge sorted files in the background. Reads may consult several files (Bloom filters help), and compaction rewrites data repeatedly.
